strengths: The main result of the paper lies in developing a generalization of the existing generative models into one theoretical framework, with a universal characterization of generators provided by Theorem 1, stated for time‑inhomogeneous Markov processes, and demonstrated by designing two new generative models based on jump and diffusion processes.

Overall, the paper is well‑executed and well‑written, providing necessary background into Feller processes, offering motivation and intuition behind introduced mathematical concepts, giving concise guidance principles to build new generative models, and presenting a mathematically sound and computationally feasible generator matching framework supported by empirical results on protein and image generation.

The introduction of jump, a type of stochastic process in the continuous domain with non‑continuous trajectories, largely unexplored within the generative AI community, and the result showing that the widely‑used conditional path can also be achieved through jumps, highlighting its potential utility for generative tasks.

An elegant theorem establishing that the generators of interest in ℝ^d for applications can be decomposed into three basic types: flow (ODE), diffusion (scaled Brownian motion), and jump, underscoring the advantages of using the generator perspective in modeling.

The paper introduces methodologies for combining models that use different generators and for modeling multimodal data; while not entirely novel, these contributions effectively systematize existing techniques through the GM perspective.
The paper is well‑written, featuring clear notations, a strong motivation, and a rigorous mathematical foundation.

This paper has the ambitious goal of presenting a unifying framework for many currently popular generative modeling paradigms, including continuous and discrete models and jump processes, which can be very relevant for the community, and the theory seems adequate and well supported.
Experiments are performed on diverse applications: proteins and images.

The authors introduce a unified framework that combines a unified theory to explain how distinct Markov processes, defined across various state spaces, can be represented within a consistent language, and exploit this framework to propose a novel generator‑based parameterization that offers a streamlined and theoretically grounded approach to model various Markov processes in a consistent fashion.

Beyond recovering existing diffusion‑based models within the unified framework, the paper uses this framework to establish innovative classes of generative models, for example by straightforwardly combining different types of Markov processes, paving the way for flexible yet rigorous generative modeling approaches.

The paper provides invaluable insights for comprehensively understanding various diffusion‑based models (including flow matching, bridge matching, and others), offering a cohesive view that can unify these models within a broader framework and could become a must‑read for those interested in this topic.
weaknesses: The authors ignore previous results that have been done for jump processes [1, 2]; they should provide a very detailed comparison with these papers in the related work section.

The exposition of the framework can be improved; it remains unclear why the generator L_t can be used in forward and reverse processes and why using generators and adjoint KFE leads to “correct” generated samples.
The authors skip a discussion of Anderson’s result [3], an important brick in developing generative diffusion models, without explaining why it is not needed in the general framework.
It is unclear why regularity assumption 2 (finite number of discontinuities) is needed; the authors discard one term in the proof of Theorem 1, and the impact of keeping that term is not explained.
The authors claim that generator matching works with arbitrary Markov processes while in reality they restrict to Feller processes, raising the question whether the restriction may be unnecessary.
In Proposition 1, the “conditional generator” appears without any definition, and the object X^z_t is introduced for the first time without definition.
The paper does not provide a motivation behind introducing the three regularity assumptions on the Markov process under consideration.
Page 3, line 120: the meaning (or definition) of “right” in the phrase “Starting with the right initial distribution X₀ ∼ p₀” is unclear.
Page 3, lines 96‑99: the meaning of δ_z(dx) is not defined before nor in the formula.
The phrase “an informal” in lines 129‑130 is unclear.
Page 17, lines 762‑763: typo “the following two regularity …” should be “the following three regularity …”.

The writing style in some parts, especially Section 6, feels overly general and abstract; the framework primarily applies to only four specific examples, and the theoretical constructs (e.g., target‑affine loss and Bregman divergences) lack practical utility and illustrative examples, limiting the reader’s ability to grasp the practical impact.

The literature review for jump‑based models is insufficient; related works on piecewise deterministic processes and piecewise diffusion processes, as well as recent papers such as Campbell et al. (2023) and Bertazzi et al. (2024), are not mentioned.

The experiments are not convincing enough and lack design details needed for fair comparisons, including unclear recommendations for conditional probability paths, missing comparisons on more complex targets, insufficient details on image generation setup, outdated baselines, absence of multimodal generation results, and missing important metrics and recent baselines for protein experiments.

It is unclear how the GM framework offers benefits over simple, naive combinations of different modeling paradigms, and the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate practical advantages beyond theoretical unification.

The limitations of the GM framework are not clearly discussed; the requirement that operators be “simple” and linear may restrict the ability to capture highly non‑linear data distributions, and the trade‑offs between mathematical tractability and modeling power are not explored.

Figure 2 lacks clarity: the abbreviation “ME” in the legend is undefined, the text is too small, and the legend naming does not match the vertical naming of the rows, making the figure difficult to understand.

The dual interpretation of p_t as both a measure function and a function on S creates confusion and leads to inconsistent notation, including the unnecessary operator ⊙, which should be replaced by a standard inner product and defined via a density (Radon‑Nikodym derivative).

The notational issues undermine the motivation for using the F‑parameterization rather than directly parameterizing the generator ℒ; a clearer formulation (e.g., expressing generator matching in terms of inner products) would clarify the advantage of the F‑parameterization.
The notational inconsistencies risk widespread misunderstanding if left unresolved, and the reviewer is inclined to assign a lower score until they are thoroughly addressed.
